questions.question: You run a 50-task eval once: 66% before a change, 62% after. What can you conclude?
options: The change made the agent worse
Very little: one run per task varies by several points with no change at all
questions.explanation: In the lesson, the same agent scored 62%–70% across five identical runs.

questions.question: A task succeeded 7 of 10 times. What are pass@3 and pass^3 roughly?
questions.explanation: At least one of three almost always works; all three working happens under a third of the time.

questions.question: Why compare agents with a paired bootstrap over tasks?
options: Both agents saw the same tasks, so pairing removes task-difficulty noise, and resampling tasks gives an interval on the difference
Bootstrap always says B is better
It needs fewer trials than any other method
questions.explanation: The question is about the difference, so put the interval on the difference.

questions.question: With 1 trial per task, the truly better agent B scored lower than A. What did the bootstrap say?
options: Can't tell: the interval on the difference included zero
questions.explanation: An honest interval stops you from acting on noise.

questions.question: Which metric fits a customer-support agent where every conversation must work?
questions.explanation: Users don't get best-of-k; reliability across attempts is what they feel.

questions.question: An agent looks up prices in a different order than the reference but gets the right total. How should it be graded?
options: Fail: the trajectory doesn't match exactly
Pass on outcome, with checks only on path constraints that matter (required or forbidden calls)
questions.explanation: Exact-path matching produces false failures; grade outcomes and constrain the path where it matters.
